id_and_class.summary: Halligan and Oakley argue that subjective awareness is an epiphenomenon, an inner feeling with no causal power, generated by the brain alongside outputs that fast non-conscious systems have already produced. Selected outputs are internally broadcast as a personal narrative, and the evolved purpose of this broadcast is to let people share its contents with others, supporting sociality, the human species' central survival strategy.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Consciousness as a Causally Inert Social Broadcast

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Halligan and Oakley define consciousness as embodied subjective awareness including meta-cognition. They identify it as a brain-generated accompaniment to selected outputs of non-conscious processing, felt but without causal power.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Both conscious and non-conscious aspects of mind depend on neural processes. The brain does the work, and awareness is a by-product that cannot act back on brain or behaviour.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Weak emergence (a by-product of evolved neurocognitive architecture)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Subjective awareness is a self-referential personal narrative built from selected thoughts, sensations, intentions, beliefs, memories, and emotions. The feeling that this narrative directs action is an intuition, and the authors argue it is false.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Qualia are real as experiences and valued by the individual, but they are end products of unconscious processing with no influence on what happens next.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Brains, non-conscious neurocognitive systems, an internal broadcasting process, and social groups through which beliefs and feelings are culturally transmitted.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Through cognitive neuroscience over the past three decades, which the authors read as showing that executive functions run without awareness, together with study of how intuitive lay theories shape beliefs about the mind.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: A large evolved architecture of fast non-conscious systems whose selected outputs are broadcast into a continuously updated personal narrative.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal, Meta-cognition, Agency (as felt but non-causal), Self-narrative
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Internal broadcasting: non-conscious systems select some of their outputs and broadcast them as the contents of experience. That broadcast exists so its contents can be externally broadcast to other people.
mechanism_and_dynamics.dynamics_of_emergence: The personal narrative is updated continuously after the fact, as outputs arrive from unconscious processing; awareness never steers that updating.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Generated by the brain's evolved neurocognitive architecture; no single region is specified.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Consciousness itself has no causal role. The unconscious processes that produce it serve collective social communication and harmony through cultural transmission of beliefs, feelings, ideas, and behaviours.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Information flows one way, from non-conscious systems into the conscious narrative and from there, by those same systems, out to other people. Awareness is a mental representation lacking the neurocognitive capacity to influence other processes.
mechanism_and_dynamics.evolutionary_account: Much of the mind's architecture evolved to serve sociality, the human tendency to form social links and live in communities. Subjective awareness evolved for humans as social beings, echoing Nietzsche's remark that consciousness is a net of communication between people.
core_claims_and_evidence: Executive functions usually attributed to awareness are carried out by fast, efficient non-conscious brain systems, according to the authors' reading of cognitive neuroscience.
Belief in mental causation stems from intuitive mind-body dualism found across cultures and in young children, and it persists because legal, political, and moral institutions endorse it daily.
Both the contents and the experience of consciousness are end products of unconscious processes.
Free will, justice, and moral responsibility make sense when attributed to persons in a social community, even if not to an assembly of nerve cells.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Empirical (cognitive neuroscience) combined with evolutionary and philosophical argument

empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: If awareness has no causal powers, natural selection could not have selected it for its own effects, so the evolutionary story has to rest on the underlying processes. The view also clashes with strong intuitions of free will and agency, which the authors treat as scientific misconceptions to be revised.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: The account does not explain why the brain should generate felt experience at all if non-conscious systems already do the work. How social institutions should adjust to a non-causal view of awareness is left open.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Consistent with a physicalist picture of the brain, though epiphenomenalism raises the familiar puzzle of how we can talk and write about experiences that cause nothing.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Since awareness is a by-product of brain processes, it ends when the brain does.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: Halligan and Oakley locate the value of experience and of social realities such as morality and democracy in persons living in communities, with no cosmic purpose.

related_theories.name: Baars's and Dehaene's Global Workspace Theory
